title: Architecture from requirements
principle: Architecture begins with the user outcome, data boundary, and operating constraint. A model choice is one part of the design, not the design itself.
mechanism: Translate requirements into a request path, trust boundaries, data flow, failure behavior, and measurable acceptance checks. Map each requirement to a component that owns it.

decision.when: Use this skill when requirements span model quality, latency, data access, operations, or deployment.
decision.choice: Choose a managed inference path or a hosted model path from the required control and operating capacity.
decision.reason: The choice must meet the use case and constraints together.
decision.reject: Reject a model-first design that ignores identity, data freshness, or failure recovery.

workedTrace: A business owner requires answers from current internal policy.
The architect identifies source authority, user access, and answer latency needs.
The design selects retrieval, model inference, identity filters, and monitoring.
A test question checks evidence, access, and response behavior end to end.

failure.symptom: The design meets a feature request but fails a data or latency constraint.
failure.check: Trace each requirement through a component and acceptance test.
failure.fix: Revise the path that fails, then rerun the requirement test.

experiment.change: Change the retrieval path from unrestricted to identity-filtered access in an illustrative design.
experiment.observe: Observe whether allowed questions retain evidence and denied records stay out of model input.
experiment.limit: This checks one access boundary. It does not prove every policy or traffic condition.

masteryQuestion: An illustrative assistant must answer from current internal guidance. What must architecture specify before model choice?
masteryAnswer: Specify authoritative sources, caller identity, retrieval controls, answer checks, latency needs, and failure behavior.

title: Proof of concept
principle: A proof of concept tests uncertain assumptions before a team commits to full deployment.
mechanism: Keep the prototype narrow. Use representative inputs, a defined success measure, and the intended service path where possible.

decision.when: Use this skill when feasibility, quality, service fit, or business value remains uncertain.
decision.choice: Build a small end-to-end slice that exercises the riskiest assumption.
decision.reason: A representative slice can expose integration limits earlier than a model-only demo.
decision.reject: Reject a polished demo that uses hand-picked inputs and no acceptance criteria.

workedTrace: An illustrative team doubts whether policy retrieval can support a support workflow.
It selects representative questions and expected source passages.
It connects a small corpus to retrieval and one inference route.
Reviewers compare answer evidence, errors, latency, and required operations.

failure.symptom: The demo looks useful but fails on ordinary or difficult cases.
failure.check: Compare test inputs with actual workload categories and edge cases.
failure.fix: Expand or revise the test set before drawing a scale conclusion.

experiment.change: Change the PoC corpus from curated examples to a representative approved sample.
experiment.observe: Observe retrieval coverage, answer quality, and integration defects.
experiment.limit: A PoC cannot establish production capacity or prove every risk is controlled.

masteryQuestion: Why can a successful model playground demo fail as a proof of concept?
masteryAnswer: It may omit the real data, identity, retrieval, application path, and measurable acceptance criteria.

title: Standardized components
principle: Standard components reduce variation across applications while preserving explicit choices for different requirements.
mechanism: Define reusable interfaces, security defaults, observability fields, deployment patterns, and review checks. Use a framework such as the Generative AI Lens to assess design areas.

decision.when: Use this skill when teams build similar model features in multiple deployment scenarios.
decision.choice: Publish a reference component with documented extension points and controls.
decision.reason: Teams can repeat known safeguards and focus review on deliberate deviations.
decision.reject: Reject a single rigid template that cannot express different data or latency requirements.

workedTrace: A platform team sees repeated model invocation code.
It defines a shared request adapter and identity requirements.
Teams adopt the component and document approved variations.
A design review checks the shared defaults and each exception.

failure.symptom: Applications call the same model service with different unreviewed policies.
failure.check: Compare deployed patterns against the component contract and approved exceptions.
failure.fix: Update the component or close unexplained gaps before rollout.

experiment.change: Change an example application to use the shared invocation component.
experiment.observe: Observe whether request validation, telemetry, and identity controls match the standard.
experiment.limit: A standard component cannot ensure correct use if teams bypass it or supply poor data.

masteryQuestion: What should a shared component standardize, and what should remain configurable?
masteryAnswer: Standardize stable interfaces and safeguards. Keep model, data, and workload choices configurable with reviewed limits.

title: Foundation model choice
principle: Choose a foundation model by demonstrated fit for a defined task and operating constraints.
mechanism: Compare capability, modality, limitations, supported settings, access, Region, output quality, and latency on representative cases.

decision.when: Use this skill when several models could perform the same application task.
decision.choice: Run a comparative evaluation against the workload acceptance criteria.
decision.reason: Measured task behavior gives stronger evidence than general reputation.
decision.reject: Reject a choice based only on a benchmark or a single successful prompt.

workedTrace: An illustrative team needs extraction from support messages.
It defines expected fields and failure costs.
It tests candidate models with the same examples and request shape.
It compares correctness, refusal behavior, latency, and supported operation.

failure.symptom: A model scores well overall but fails a high-impact task category.
failure.check: Review per-category failures and current model constraints.
failure.fix: Choose a model that passes the critical criteria or revise the workflow.

experiment.change: Change only the candidate model while holding the test set and prompt fixed.
experiment.observe: Observe task quality, latency, and output validity by category.
experiment.limit: Evaluation results apply to the tested task, prompt, and model configuration.

masteryQuestion: Why is the highest general benchmark score not enough to select a model?
masteryAnswer: It may not reflect this workload, required modality, constraints, or critical failure categories.

title: Provider and model switching
principle: A flexible architecture separates application intent from provider-specific request details.
mechanism: Use a stable internal request contract and adapters that map it to supported provider APIs. Centralize route configuration outside business logic where suitable.

decision.when: Use this skill when an application must change model route or provider with limited code changes.
decision.choice: Introduce an adapter and controlled route configuration.
decision.reason: This limits code coupling and supports policy-based route changes.
decision.reject: Reject the claim that one common API makes model behavior identical.

workedTrace: A client sends a task through an internal model interface.
Configuration selects an approved provider route.
An adapter maps the task to that route’s request format.
The response maps back to the application result contract.

failure.symptom: A route switch causes missing fields or different answer behavior.
failure.check: Check adapter mapping, supported settings, and evaluation for the new route.
failure.fix: Add explicit route-specific handling and rerun contract tests.

experiment.change: Change the configured route to a second approved model without editing business logic.
experiment.observe: Observe request validity and answer contract behavior for both routes.
experiment.limit: Switching still requires model-specific evaluation and may need adapter updates.

masteryQuestion: What does a provider abstraction simplify, and what does it not standardize?
masteryAnswer: It simplifies routing and request mapping. It does not standardize capability or output behavior.

title: Resilient inference design
principle: Resilience keeps a useful service path available when a dependency fails or becomes unavailable.
mechanism: Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, cross-Region options, or graceful degradation according to the failure mode.

decision.when: Use this skill when inference availability or regional capacity is a business requirement.
decision.choice: Choose a fallback that preserves an acceptable user outcome and policy boundary.
decision.reason: A controlled fallback can prevent cascading failure while exposing reduced capability.
decision.reject: Reject unbounded retries or silent fallback to an untested model.

workedTrace: A primary inference route returns repeated transient errors.
The application classifies the error and opens its circuit after the configured condition.
A permitted fallback route or safe degraded response serves the request.
Telemetry records the route and later recovery.

failure.symptom: Retries amplify load or fallback answers break the response contract.
failure.check: Inspect error class, retry count, circuit state, and fallback evaluation.
failure.fix: Bound retries and validate each fallback against the same task needs.

experiment.change: Change the circuit-breaker threshold or fallback route in a test configuration.
experiment.observe: Observe recovery time, failed calls, and fallback answer suitability.
experiment.limit: A fallback cannot guarantee identical quality, region, or feature support.

masteryQuestion: Why must a fallback route be evaluated before an outage?
masteryAnswer: It can differ in capability and output behavior, so the application must validate its safe use in advance.

title: Customized model lifecycle
principle: A customized model needs controlled versioning, deployment, evaluation, and retirement.
mechanism: Track training or adaptation inputs, model artifact, deployment configuration, evaluation, and rollback path. Use a registry and automated release process where applicable.

decision.when: Use this skill when a base model does not meet a validated domain requirement and customization is justified.
decision.choice: Deploy a versioned customized artifact through a tested pipeline.
decision.reason: Traceability supports comparison, rollback, and later retirement.
decision.reject: Reject an untracked model replacement based only on a promising sample.

workedTrace: A domain task shows a stable capability gap after prompt and retrieval checks.
The team prepares a customization dataset and records its provenance.
It registers and deploys a candidate model version.
Evaluation gates promotion and preserves a rollback target.

failure.symptom: A new deployment regresses quality or cannot be tied to its training data.
failure.check: Compare artifact, data lineage, evaluation, and deployment versions.
failure.fix: Restore the last approved version and repair the release record.

experiment.change: Change the deployment from the current registered model version to a candidate version.
experiment.observe: Observe task quality, endpoint behavior, and rollback readiness.
experiment.limit: Customization does not remove the need for data rights, evaluation, or lifecycle review.

masteryQuestion: What evidence should support promotion of a customized model?
masteryAnswer: Versioned artifact and data lineage, task evaluation, deployment checks, owner approval, and rollback readiness.

title: Input data validation
principle: Validation catches data defects before they affect model behavior.
mechanism: Check schema, required fields, types, ranges, missing values, duplicates, and domain rules. Send failures to a visible correction path.

decision.when: Use this skill before inference when input quality affects answer correctness or safety.
decision.choice: Validate at ingestion and again at the application boundary for changing inputs.
decision.reason: Early checks reduce downstream ambiguity and make defects easier to locate.
decision.reject: Reject reliance on the model to repair malformed or missing facts silently.

workedTrace: An illustrative workflow receives tabular customer requests.
A validation stage checks required columns and allowed formats.
Valid rows proceed to feature or prompt preparation.
Invalid rows are quarantined with an actionable error record.

failure.symptom: The model produces inconsistent answers from malformed inputs.
failure.check: Inspect validation results and compare source values with prompt values.
failure.fix: Correct upstream records or reject invalid input before inference.

experiment.change: Change a required-field rule from permissive to explicit rejection in a test flow.
experiment.observe: Observe invalid-row counts and downstream answer errors.
experiment.limit: A validation rule can reject valid exceptions if domain rules are incomplete.

masteryQuestion: Why should data checks run before inference?
masteryAnswer: They prevent malformed or missing values from becoming ambiguous model input and support a clear correction path.

title: Multimodal data processing
principle: Each modality needs processing that preserves information needed by the task.
mechanism: Images, audio, video, text, and tables have different parsing and representation needs. Use suitable services or model inputs for each type.

decision.when: Use this skill when the source contains more than plain text or a specialized content form.
decision.choice: Build a modality-aware path and retain links to original source objects.
decision.reason: The path can extract the relevant structure without treating every file as plain text.
decision.reject: Reject lossy conversion that drops labels, timing, layout, or source identity.

workedTrace: An illustrative case receives an audio support recording and an image attachment.
The workflow transcribes audio and extracts relevant image content.
It associates both outputs with the case identifier.
The model receives task-relevant content with source references.

failure.symptom: The model misses a table value or an audio detail lost in conversion.
failure.check: Inspect extracted content and compare it with the original artifact.
failure.fix: Change parsing or modality handling before adjusting the model prompt.

experiment.change: Change the preprocessing route for one modality while keeping the task constant.
experiment.observe: Observe extracted fields, omissions, and downstream response correctness.
experiment.limit: Extraction quality depends on source clarity and the selected processing path.

masteryQuestion: Why should image and audio inputs use modality-aware preprocessing?
masteryAnswer: Their structure and useful signals differ from plain text and can be lost through generic conversion.

title: Model-specific input formatting
principle: Valid input formatting is part of model integration, not cosmetic cleanup.
mechanism: Serialize roles, content blocks, parameters, and structured data according to the selected model API. Validate the request before invocation.

decision.when: Use this skill whenever the application sends prompts, messages, tables, or structured payloads.
decision.choice: Build the request from a typed internal representation and model-specific serializer.
decision.reason: This catches shape errors while keeping business data separate from transport details.
decision.reject: Reject manually concatenated JSON or assumptions that all models accept the same fields.

workedTrace: The application stores a user question and system policy separately.
A serializer maps them to supported message roles and content blocks.
The API validates and invokes the model.
The response parser extracts expected content and usage state.

failure.symptom: The service rejects a request or the application misreads returned content.
failure.check: Compare serialized body against the API contract and model support.
failure.fix: Fix the serializer or response parser, then rerun boundary tests.

experiment.change: Change one message field to the documented format for the selected API.
experiment.observe: Observe request validation and parsed output shape.
experiment.limit: A valid request shape does not prove the generated content is correct.

masteryQuestion: What should an application verify before it sends an inference request?
masteryAnswer: It should verify required fields, roles, content structure, supported settings, and model-specific constraints.

title: Input data quality enhancement
principle: Data enhancement makes source content clearer or more consistent before inference.
mechanism: Normalize formatting, extract entities, remove irrelevant markup, or reformat text while preserving meaning and provenance.

decision.when: Use this skill when noisy or inconsistent inputs reduce model consistency.
decision.choice: Apply deterministic transformations first and use model assistance only for tasks that need it.
decision.reason: Deterministic normalization is easier to inspect and reproduce.
decision.reject: Reject enhancement that silently changes facts or discards source context.

workedTrace: A source contains inconsistent date formats and copied markup.
A normalizer standardizes dates and removes irrelevant markup.
An entity step extracts names while retaining source references.
The model receives cleaner content and a trace to the original.

failure.symptom: Cleaned text changes a value or removes a qualifying phrase.
failure.check: Compare transformed fields with the original source and transformation logs.
failure.fix: Correct the transformation and add a preservation check.

experiment.change: Change one normalization rule for date or markup handling.
experiment.observe: Observe field consistency and preservation of original meaning.
experiment.limit: Normalization can improve input form but cannot establish source truth.

masteryQuestion: How can a team improve text quality without losing evidence?
masteryAnswer: Apply traceable transformations, preserve original values and provenance, and validate semantic preservation.

title: Vector database architecture
principle: A vector architecture must connect source content, embeddings, metadata, retrieval, and model context.
mechanism: Choose managed knowledge base or custom storage based on integration, query, scale, filter, and operational needs. Keep source records authoritative.

decision.when: Use this skill when semantic retrieval augments model answers over organizational data.
decision.choice: Design the ingestion and query path together, including permissions and update behavior.
decision.reason: The index is useful only when it returns authorized, relevant, current content.
decision.reject: Reject a vector store selection based only on similarity search support.

workedTrace: A source document is parsed and split into retrievable records.
Each record receives an embedding and source metadata.
A query retrieves records under trusted filters.
The application adds selected evidence and source references to the model request.

failure.symptom: Relevant documents exist but retrieval returns stale or inaccessible records.
failure.check: Inspect ingestion state, metadata, filters, and retrieved passages.
failure.fix: Fix the broken stage instead of replacing the model first.

experiment.change: Change the managed or custom retrieval path for one controlled dataset.
experiment.observe: Observe update behavior, filter correctness, and evidence relevance.
experiment.limit: Vector stores do not enforce every document rule unless the system applies those controls.

masteryQuestion: What must a vector architecture define beyond storage choice?
masteryAnswer: It must define ingestion, embeddings, metadata, access filters, retrieval, freshness, and source traceability.

title: Metadata framework
principle: Metadata gives retrieved content context such as source, date, author, type, and access scope.
mechanism: Define field names, types, trusted origins, allowed filters, and update rules. Preserve metadata through parsing and indexing.

decision.when: Use this skill when recency, authorship, domain, or access scope affects retrieval.
decision.choice: Create a small governed schema tied to real query and policy needs.
decision.reason: Consistent metadata supports filtering and interpretation.
decision.reject: Reject arbitrary tags that lack a producer or clear use.

workedTrace: A policy source has a department and revision date.
Ingestion extracts or receives those attributes from a trusted source.
A query applies a caller-authorized department filter.
The result retains revision and source identity for answer review.

failure.symptom: A relevant record is filtered out or an unauthorized record appears.
failure.check: Check field mapping, source trust, and filter derivation.
failure.fix: Repair metadata generation and enforce filters from authenticated context.

experiment.change: Change the metadata schema to include a trusted document-status field.
experiment.observe: Observe retrieval of current approved records and exclusion of obsolete ones.
experiment.limit: Metadata filters work only when fields are correctly populated and supported.

masteryQuestion: Why is metadata governance part of retrieval design?
masteryAnswer: Filters and context rely on stable, trusted values that preserve source meaning and access boundaries.

title: High-performance vector architecture
principle: Search performance depends on index design, query load, data shape, and retrieval requirements.
mechanism: Use workload measurements to guide sharding, index separation, and hierarchical approaches where supported. Keep relevance and freshness checks alongside speed.

decision.when: Use this skill when retrieval scale or response time threatens an application objective.
decision.choice: Measure the bottleneck first, then adjust the relevant index or query structure.
decision.reason: A targeted change avoids adding complexity where the model or network is actually slow.
decision.reject: Reject sharding or multiple indices as automatic performance fixes.

workedTrace: A retrieval service shows slow results on a growing corpus.
Tracing shows index query time dominates the request.
The team tests an index layout suited to domain partitions.
It compares latency and relevant-result coverage under representative queries.

failure.symptom: Latency improves but the relevant passage is no longer returned.
failure.check: Measure retrieval latency with recall or coverage on the same test set.
failure.fix: Tune layout or query behavior until both constraints are acceptable.

experiment.change: Change a domain index partition strategy in a test copy.
experiment.observe: Observe query latency, result coverage, and operational complexity.
experiment.limit: Index tuning depends on store capabilities and actual query distribution.

masteryQuestion: What evidence should precede a vector index architecture change?
masteryAnswer: Stage-level latency and retrieval-quality data under representative query and corpus conditions.

title: Resource integration
principle: Integration connects source systems to the content and metadata used by a GenAI application.
mechanism: Use connectors, APIs, events, or scheduled jobs to ingest data with identity, change, and error handling.

decision.when: Use this skill when useful knowledge sits across document systems, wikis, or business stores.
decision.choice: Choose the integration path that preserves source authority and update signals.
decision.reason: Correct synchronization keeps downstream retrieval aligned with source state.
decision.reject: Reject bulk copying without ownership, deletion, and access rules.

workedTrace: An internal wiki publishes a revised procedure.
An integration detects the change and reads content with approved access.
The pipeline maps content and metadata into the knowledge source.
A retrieval check confirms the revised procedure is searchable.

failure.symptom: A source update never appears or the integration exposes excess content.
failure.check: Trace source permissions, change detection, mapping, and sync status.
failure.fix: Repair the integration boundary and re-run a targeted sync.

experiment.change: Change the sync trigger from a scheduled refresh to a source event in an illustrative test.
experiment.observe: Observe freshness, failed records, and access scope.
experiment.limit: Event delivery and source APIs can have limits that require backfill handling.

masteryQuestion: What should an integration preserve when it moves enterprise content?
masteryAnswer: Source identity, permissions, metadata, update and deletion state, and an auditable error path.

title: Vector store maintenance
principle: A vector index is derived data and needs refresh, correction, and deletion controls.
mechanism: Use incremental sync or scheduled refresh based on source change behavior and freshness needs. Track failures and stale records.

decision.when: Use this skill when source material changes after initial indexing.
decision.choice: Select a maintenance path that detects updates and removals reliably.
decision.reason: The retrieval system must reflect authoritative source changes.
decision.reject: Reject a one-time ingestion plan for a changing knowledge source.

workedTrace: A source owner corrects a published procedure.
The sync mechanism detects the modified source object.
The ingestion path replaces its derived index records.
A query verifies the new procedure and no obsolete clause.

failure.symptom: Users continue to receive content from an older source version.
failure.check: Compare source revision, sync result, indexed metadata, and retrieval output.
failure.fix: Retry or repair the sync, then verify replacement and deletion behavior.

experiment.change: Change the refresh trigger or schedule for a test data source.
experiment.observe: Observe update delay, failed records, and stale retrieval.
experiment.limit: The best refresh interval depends on change patterns and the use case.

masteryQuestion: Why is index freshness an application quality concern?
masteryAnswer: Answers can remain stale when derived retrieval data does not reflect current source state.

title: Document segmentation
principle: Segmentation determines which surrounding facts can travel with a retrieved passage.
mechanism: Use fixed-size, semantic, hierarchical, or custom chunking based on document structure and query needs. Preserve headers and source locations.

decision.when: Use this skill when long documents need focused retrieval.
decision.choice: Select boundaries by representative questions that require rules, exceptions, tables, or cross-section context.
decision.reason: Chunk boundaries affect both matching and final evidence completeness.
decision.reject: Reject a universal chunk size detached from content and task.

workedTrace: A policy sentence and its exception sit near a boundary.
The chunker splits the document into indexed passages.
A query retrieves the rule passage without the exception.
The answer omits the condition because it never entered context.

failure.symptom: Answers omit qualifications despite a relevant source document.
failure.check: Inspect parsed content, chunk boundaries, and returned passages.
failure.fix: Adjust boundary strategy or parent context and test again.

experiment.change: Change the chunk size or strategy for the targeted source set.
experiment.observe: Observe exception coverage, irrelevant text, and result count.
experiment.limit: Different formats and queries may need different segmentation.

masteryQuestion: Why can a highly precise small chunk still produce a wrong answer?
masteryAnswer: It may omit a nearby condition or exception needed to interpret the matched statement.

title: Embedding selection
principle: Embedding choice determines how text and queries map into a similarity space.
mechanism: Compare supported embedding models for domain fit, dimensions, language, throughput, and compatibility with the index. Re-embed when representation changes.Keep embedding identifiers attached to index versions for later comparison.

decision.when: Use this skill when selecting or changing semantic search representations.
decision.choice: Evaluate candidate embeddings on labeled retrieval queries and source passages.
decision.reason: Measured relevance reveals domain behavior more directly than vector size alone.
decision.reject: Reject mixing incompatible query and document representations.

workedTrace: Ingestion encodes each source chunk with one embedding model.
The index stores those vectors with text and metadata.
The query path embeds a question compatibly.
Similarity search returns passages that evaluation can assess.

failure.symptom: Relevant terms fail to retrieve after an embedding migration.
failure.check: Check model compatibility, index version, chunk content, and query cases.
failure.fix: Re-embed the corpus or restore the compatible query model.

experiment.change: Change the embedding model and re-index a controlled corpus.
experiment.observe: Observe retrieval relevance, query latency, and migration completeness.
experiment.limit: Embedding scores are not truth probabilities and model changes require migration planning.

masteryQuestion: What must remain compatible for meaningful vector similarity?
masteryAnswer: Document and query vectors must use compatible embedding representations and index configuration.

title: Vector search deployment
principle: Vector search deployment connects a compatible index to query and filtering operations.
mechanism: Configure vector fields, dimensions, distance behavior, metadata fields, access, and index lifecycle according to the selected store.

decision.when: Use this skill when enabling semantic search in a custom or managed retrieval path.
decision.choice: Choose a store based on supported query features and operating requirements.
decision.reason: The store must support the application’s vector, filter, and scale needs.
decision.reject: Reject a storage choice before confirming integration and query constraints.

workedTrace: The ingestion service creates a vector for each record.
The index schema accepts the vector and trusted metadata.
A query embeds user text and applies required filters.
The store returns records that the application validates and uses.

failure.symptom: Index creation succeeds but queries return errors or poor matches.
failure.check: Verify dimensions, schema, distance configuration, and filter support.
failure.fix: Align index and query configuration, then test known records.

experiment.change: Change the index schema or search configuration in a test environment.
experiment.observe: Observe query success, relevance, and filter behavior.
experiment.limit: Deployment correctness does not establish answer grounding.

masteryQuestion: What must align between vector creation and vector search?
masteryAnswer: Embedding representation, vector dimensions, index schema, and query configuration must agree.

title: Advanced search relevance
principle: Search quality can improve by combining retrieval signals and reranking candidates.
mechanism: Use lexical, semantic, hybrid, and reranking stages to address distinct retrieval defects. Keep filters and candidate trace visible.

decision.when: Use this skill when simple semantic retrieval misses exact terms or ranks evidence poorly.
decision.choice: Use hybrid retrieval for exact terms plus meaning, and rerank when candidate order is the measured issue.
decision.reason: Each stage addresses a different failure point.
decision.reject: Reject reranking as a fix for a passage absent from first-stage candidates.

workedTrace: A query contains an exact code and a natural-language description.
Semantic search returns related guidance but misses the exact record.
Hybrid search adds lexical matches and a reranker adjusts order.
Evaluation checks whether the final context contains the exact source.

failure.symptom: A reranker cannot surface the expected item.
failure.check: Inspect first-stage candidate recall before reranker output.
failure.fix: Improve lexical fields, filters, or candidate generation first.

experiment.change: Change search mode from semantic to hybrid on a supported store.
experiment.observe: Observe exact-term recall, irrelevant candidates, and final answer evidence.
experiment.limit: Hybrid support depends on the configured store and searchable text fields.

masteryQuestion: When should a team add a reranker?
masteryAnswer: When relevant candidates exist but their order remains a measured retrieval defect.

title: Query handling
principle: Query transformation can improve retrieval when user wording hides the needed search intent.
mechanism: Expand, decompose, normalize, or route queries while preserving the original question and evidence relationship.

decision.when: Use this skill when one query contains multiple issues or unfamiliar phrasing.
decision.choice: Transform only the query classes shown to fail, then compare with the original retrieval.
decision.reason: Targeted transformation can improve coverage while limiting added noise.
decision.reject: Reject untested rewriting that changes a user’s intent.

workedTrace: A question asks for two independent policy conditions.
A query step decomposes it into focused subqueries.
Each subquery retrieves its own evidence.
The application combines passages and checks both parts before generation.

failure.symptom: The rewrite retrieves related content but misses the user’s actual constraint.
failure.check: Compare original and transformed query, then inspect each result set.
failure.fix: Preserve key entities and test query-level relevance before combining results.

experiment.change: Change the query decomposition rule for multi-part questions.
experiment.observe: Observe evidence coverage for each subquestion and total retrieval noise.
experiment.limit: Transformation can add latency and can distort intent.

masteryQuestion: How can query decomposition help a multi-part question?
masteryAnswer: It can retrieve evidence for each part separately, provided the application preserves the original constraints.

title: Standard retrieval interfaces
principle: A stable retrieval interface lets applications call search without coupling every client to one store.
mechanism: Define query, filter, result, source-reference, and error contracts. Implement the adapter with a controlled API, tool, or MCP client.

decision.when: Use this skill when multiple applications or models need the same retrieval capability.
decision.choice: Expose a narrow API that returns evidence and provenance in a stable shape.
decision.reason: A stable contract supports changes behind the boundary and consistent access checks.
decision.reject: Reject a generic tool that exposes unrestricted database operations.

workedTrace: A model-connected application receives a user question.
The retrieval client sends a validated query and trusted identity filters.
The retrieval service returns passages with source identifiers and scores.
The host selects authorized context and records the result status.

failure.symptom: A client receives content without provenance or applies inconsistent filters.
failure.check: Inspect interface fields, caller identity, errors, and source links.
failure.fix: Tighten the contract and enforce shared authorization in the service.

experiment.change: Change the interface response to require a source identifier for each passage.
experiment.observe: Observe client compatibility and evidence traceability.
experiment.limit: A common interface does not eliminate store-specific limits or model behavior.

masteryQuestion: What must a retrieval contract return besides passage text?
masteryAnswer: It should return source identity, relevant metadata, status, and fields needed for safe filtering and review.

title: Instruction frameworks
principle: Instructions define task behavior, boundaries, and expected output for the model.
mechanism: Separate stable system rules from user input and retrieved evidence. Use templates, examples, output formats, and supported guardrails.

decision.when: Use this skill when model behavior or response structure needs controlled guidance.
decision.choice: Write explicit instructions and validate outputs against the application contract.
decision.reason: Clear boundaries reduce ambiguity and support repeatable evaluation.
decision.reject: Reject the assumption that prompt text enforces permissions or guarantees truth.

workedTrace: The application loads a versioned instruction template.
It inserts the task request and clearly marked evidence.
The model generates a response under those instructions.
A validator checks structure and required evidence before delivery.

failure.symptom: The model follows an instruction embedded in untrusted source text.
failure.check: Inspect prompt assembly and variable boundaries.
failure.fix: Mark external text as data and enforce permissions outside the prompt.

experiment.change: Change the template to delimit retrieved evidence explicitly.
experiment.observe: Observe instruction adherence and task quality on injection and normal cases.
experiment.limit: Prompt controls guide behavior but do not replace authorization or validation.

masteryQuestion: What does a prompt instruction framework control, and what remains external?
masteryAnswer: It guides model response behavior. Identity, permissions, truth checks, and side-effect controls remain application responsibilities.

title: Interactive context
principle: Interactive systems retain useful conversation state while keeping each turn grounded and manageable.
mechanism: Use session identifiers, bounded history, summaries, intent recognition, and clarification states. Persist only what the application needs.

decision.when: Use this skill when later turns depend on prior user context or need clarification.
decision.choice: Store task-relevant state with explicit ownership and expiry behavior.
decision.reason: State supports continuity without sending an unlimited transcript every time.
decision.reject: Reject reliance on model memory for facts absent from the current request.

workedTrace: A user asks “What about the second option?” after a comparison.
The application resolves the reference from recent session state.
It asks a clarification if the reference is ambiguous.
It sends the selected option and current evidence to inference.

failure.symptom: The assistant uses the wrong referent from an old turn.
failure.check: Inspect stored state, recency, session identity, and reference resolution.
failure.fix: Ask a clarifying question or use a bounded state summary.

experiment.change: Change the history policy from full transcript to relevant recent turns plus a summary.
experiment.observe: Observe reference resolution, token use, and correction rate.
experiment.limit: Summaries can omit facts, so preserve source state for consequential decisions.

masteryQuestion: When should an interactive system ask for clarification?
masteryAnswer: When session state does not identify the user’s intended reference with sufficient confidence.

title: Prompt governance
principle: Prompt governance controls ownership, versions, approval, use, and audit of prompts.
mechanism: Store reusable templates with parameters and versions. Record who changes them and connect versions to evaluation and release evidence.

decision.when: Use this skill when prompt changes can alter production behavior or policy.
decision.choice: Manage prompts as versioned release artifacts with review and audit records.
decision.reason: A version link supports reproduction and rollback.
decision.reject: Reject untracked edits to a production prompt.

workedTrace: An owner proposes a prompt change.
The change receives a new version and review.
Evaluation runs against that version and known cases.
The release record maps the deployed prompt to approval evidence.

failure.symptom: A production answer cannot be linked to the prompt version that produced it.
failure.check: Compare deployed prompt reference with logs and release records.
failure.fix: Version the template and capture the active identifier safely.

experiment.change: Change the approval rule to require evaluation for each new prompt version.
experiment.observe: Observe whether promotion blocks when evidence is missing.
experiment.limit: Versioning cannot guarantee quality unless test cases match actual use.

masteryQuestion: Why must an incident record identify the prompt version?
masteryAnswer: Prompt changes can alter behavior, so the version is needed to reproduce and review the response.

title: Prompt quality assurance
principle: Prompt quality assurance tests whether a prompt meets its expected task behavior.
mechanism: Use fixed evaluation cases, output validators, edge cases, regression checks, and review of failures.

decision.when: Use this skill when prompts change or output reliability matters.
decision.choice: Run regression checks against a versioned test set before release.
decision.reason: The comparison reveals behavior changes caused by prompt edits.
decision.reject: Reject a prompt review based only on one manually selected output.

workedTrace: A prompt currently extracts policy owner and effective date.
A change adds a required citation field.
The test suite runs ordinary, missing-field, and exception cases.
Reviewers compare validity and evidence against the baseline.

failure.symptom: A new prompt passes common cases but fails on missing information.
failure.check: Inspect per-case output and validator results, not only aggregate score.
failure.fix: Add the failure class to regression coverage and revise the prompt or logic.

experiment.change: Change one prompt instruction while keeping model and test set fixed.
experiment.observe: Observe schema validity, evidence support, and edge-case regressions.
experiment.limit: Evaluation quality depends on case coverage and explicit expected outcomes.

masteryQuestion: What makes a prompt regression test useful?
masteryAnswer: It uses repeatable cases with expected behavior and exposes failures caused by a prompt change.

title: Iterative prompt improvement
principle: Prompt improvement is a controlled cycle of diagnosing a defect, changing a prompt, and measuring the result.
mechanism: Use structured input, examples, output constraints, decomposition, or feedback where they address a specific failure.

decision.when: Use this skill when a capable model repeatedly misses a format or task requirement.
decision.choice: Change the smallest prompt element tied to the observed error.
decision.reason: A focused change makes the cause of improvement or regression clearer.
decision.reject: Reject adding elaborate reasoning instructions without diagnosing the failure.

workedTrace: The model understands a task but returns inconsistent field names.
The team defines a schema and a representative example.
It changes the prompt and validates output after inference.
Evaluation compares format and answer correctness.

failure.symptom: Formatting improves while factual quality declines.
failure.check: Measure both format and task correctness across the same cases.
failure.fix: Keep the change only if it meets the complete acceptance criteria.

experiment.change: Add a structured output specification to the existing prompt.
experiment.observe: Observe parse success, missing fields, and semantic correctness.
experiment.limit: Prompt improvements can trade off against other behavior and need regression tests.

masteryQuestion: How should a team refine a prompt after a repeated defect?
masteryAnswer: Identify the defect, make one focused change, and compare all relevant quality measures.

title: Complex prompt systems
principle: Complex prompt systems use multiple stages, reusable components, and conditional paths.
mechanism: Separate preprocessing, prompt stages, branching rules, postprocessing, and error handling. Pass explicit state between stages.

decision.when: Use this skill when a task needs sequential prompts or conditional processing.
decision.choice: Use a workflow with visible state and branches rather than one opaque prompt.
decision.reason: Stages make decisions inspectable and let each step handle a defined purpose.
decision.reject: Reject a chain that repeats model calls without a measurable need.

workedTrace: A request first needs intent classification.
The workflow routes a policy question to retrieval and an extraction task to parsing.
Each branch applies its prompt and validates its result.
A final stage combines accepted outputs into the response.

failure.symptom: A later stage uses stale or incompatible output from an earlier stage.
failure.check: Inspect stage inputs, outputs, branch conditions, and prompt versions.
failure.fix: Validate state contracts between stages and test each branch.

experiment.change: Change a branch condition for one task class in a test workflow.
experiment.observe: Observe branch selection, intermediate validity, and total request behavior.
experiment.limit: More stages add latency, cost, and failure points.

masteryQuestion: When is a multi-stage prompt system justified?
masteryAnswer: When distinct steps or branches improve a measured outcome and each stage has a clear contract.

title: Agent memory and state
principle: Agent memory is application-managed context and state, not a guaranteed model capability.
mechanism: Store session state, task progress, and durable facts with explicit scope, retention, and retrieval rules.

decision.when: Use this skill when an agent must continue across turns or coordinate multiple agents.
decision.choice: Separate short-term conversation state from durable task memory.
decision.reason: Clear state types reduce stale or cross-session context.
decision.reject: Reject sending every prior message or sharing memory across users without access checks.

workedTrace: A user starts a multi-step task and receives a session identity.
The agent stores task status and relevant references under that session.
A later request retrieves only that session’s permitted state.
The agent resumes from verified state and updates its progress.

failure.symptom: The agent repeats work or recalls another session’s data.
failure.check: Check session keys, ownership, expiry, and persisted state contents.
failure.fix: Scope memory by identity and task, then validate state before reuse.

experiment.change: Change the memory lookup from global to session-scoped state.
experiment.observe: Observe continuation accuracy and cross-session isolation.
experiment.limit: Memory can be stale or incomplete and must remain subject to authorization.

masteryQuestion: Why should agent memory use explicit session scope?
masteryAnswer: It supports continuity while reducing stale context and cross-user data exposure.

title: Structured problem solving
principle: Structured reasoning decomposes a complex objective into steps with observable inputs and results.
mechanism: Use a planned workflow, tool observations, and decision points. Treat internal reasoning text as separate from verified evidence.

decision.when: Use this skill when a request has dependent subtasks or needs conditional execution.
decision.choice: Represent steps and evidence in an explicit workflow such as a state machine.
decision.reason: Explicit states support control, retry, audit, and recovery.
decision.reject: Reject reliance on hidden reasoning as proof that a task step occurred.

workedTrace: A request requires identifying an account and checking eligibility.
The workflow resolves the account from an approved tool.
A decision state checks eligibility from returned facts.
The workflow produces an answer or asks for missing information.

failure.symptom: The model claims a step was completed without a tool result.
failure.check: Inspect state transitions and tool observations.
failure.fix: Require verified outputs before advancing dependent steps.

experiment.change: Change the workflow to require an eligibility result before response generation.
experiment.observe: Observe whether the agent stops or asks when evidence is missing.
experiment.limit: Reasoning structure does not guarantee correct evidence or safe tool use.

masteryQuestion: What should a later step use as evidence that an earlier step succeeded?
masteryAnswer: A validated tool or workflow result, not a model statement that the step occurred.

title: Safeguarded agent workflows
principle: Agent safeguards constrain actions, runtime, resources, and recovery paths.
mechanism: Set stopping conditions, timeouts, IAM boundaries, validation, and circuit breakers around model-selected steps.

decision.when: Use this skill whenever an agent can call tools or run for multiple steps.
decision.choice: Enforce limits in workflow and service code, outside model instructions.
decision.reason: Runtime controls remain effective when the model behaves unexpectedly.
decision.reject: Reject prompt-only controls for permissions or execution limits.

workedTrace: The agent receives a request and can call a bounded tool.
A workflow checks the allowed state and remaining execution budget.
A timeout or denied IAM action stops an unsafe path.
The user receives a controlled response and an audit event.

failure.symptom: An agent loops, exceeds time, or invokes a resource outside its role.
failure.check: Inspect step count, timeout, IAM policy, and circuit state.
failure.fix: Add an enforced bound and narrow the execution role.

experiment.change: Change the workflow stop condition or timeout in a test environment.
experiment.observe: Observe termination, denied actions, and safe user response.
experiment.limit: Controls may interrupt valid tasks and need clear recovery behavior.

masteryQuestion: Where should an agent’s resource boundary be enforced?
masteryAnswer: In IAM and runtime controls that authorize each operation, not only in the prompt.

title: Model coordination
principle: Model coordination assigns work to models or capabilities and combines their results.
mechanism: Route specialized tasks to suitable models and define an aggregation rule that handles disagreement or missing output.

decision.when: Use this skill when one model or capability does not meet all task needs.
decision.choice: Coordinate only where specialization improves an evaluated outcome.
decision.reason: An explicit aggregator can preserve evidence and expose conflicts.
decision.reject: Reject an ensemble that votes without a rule for confidence or disagreement.

workedTrace: A workflow needs extraction and a policy interpretation.
A specialized model extracts fields from source content.
A second route evaluates policy against those fields and evidence.
An aggregator checks required fields and reports unresolved conflicts.

failure.symptom: The combined answer hides disagreement or propagates a bad intermediate result.
failure.check: Inspect each model result and aggregation rule.
failure.fix: Validate intermediate outputs and define conflict handling.

experiment.change: Change one task route to a specialized model while retaining the same aggregate checks.
experiment.observe: Observe per-stage quality, disagreement, latency, and total cost.
experiment.limit: Multiple models add complexity and do not guarantee better results.

masteryQuestion: When should a team coordinate multiple models?
masteryAnswer: When distinct capabilities improve measured task performance enough to justify added cost and failure paths.

title: Human collaboration
principle: Human review adds expertise or approval where automated output needs oversight.
mechanism: Route uncertain, high-impact, or consequential outcomes to a reviewer with evidence and a clear decision action.

decision.when: Use this skill when a person must validate content or authorize an action.
decision.choice: Insert a defined review state before the consequential step.
decision.reason: A human can assess context that automated checks may not capture.
decision.reject: Reject vague “human in the loop” designs without authority or workflow state.

workedTrace: An agent prepares a proposed account change.
The workflow displays the proposed change and source evidence to a reviewer.
The reviewer approves or rejects with a recorded decision.
Only an approval state permits the authorized tool call.

failure.symptom: The system performs an action before review or cannot identify who approved it.
failure.check: Check workflow order, reviewer identity, decision record, and action gate.
failure.fix: Move the action behind an explicit approval state.

experiment.change: Change the workflow to require approval before a write operation.
experiment.observe: Observe blocked actions without approval and traceable completion with approval.
experiment.limit: Review can add delay and depends on clear evidence and reviewer responsibility.

masteryQuestion: What must a human review step control?
masteryAnswer: It must provide decision authority, relevant evidence, recorded outcome, and a gate before the consequential action.

title: Reliable tool integration
principle: Tool integration turns model requests into validated application operations.
mechanism: Define narrow tool schemas, validate arguments, authorize each call, handle errors, and return useful observations.

decision.when: Use this skill when a model needs external data or application actions.
decision.choice: Expose task-specific tools rather than broad general-purpose access.
decision.reason: Narrow tools reduce invalid arguments and limit side effects.
decision.reject: Reject direct execution of unvalidated model-generated arguments.

workedTrace: The model requests a customer lookup with an identifier.
The host validates the identifier and caller permission.
A tool executes the read and returns a structured result.
The host passes a bounded observation back to the model.

failure.symptom: The tool acts on the wrong record or repeats a side effect.
failure.check: Inspect schema validation, identity checks, idempotency, and tool result.
failure.fix: Reject invalid calls before execution and verify write outcomes.

experiment.change: Change a tool schema to require a validated resource identifier.
experiment.observe: Observe invalid-call rejection and successful result structure.
experiment.limit: Model tool selection can be wrong even when the tool itself works.

masteryQuestion: What should the host do before executing a model tool request?
masteryAnswer: Validate its schema and authorize the caller and requested resource before the operation.

title: MCP extension frameworks
principle: MCP provides a standardized pattern for exposing tools and resources to connected clients.
mechanism: Choose a lightweight server for narrow stateless operations or a managed container path for complex tools. Secure server identity, transport, and outputs.

decision.when: Use this skill when tools need reusable discovery and access across model clients.
decision.choice: Build an MCP server with explicit tool contracts and client-side policy.
decision.reason: The boundary supports reuse while leaving authorization and validation explicit.
decision.reject: Reject assuming protocol standardization makes every server safe.

workedTrace: A client discovers a tool from an MCP server.
It receives the tool schema and offers it to the model.
The host validates the requested arguments and server access.
The server returns data that the host treats as untrusted input.

failure.symptom: A server exposes excessive tools or returns content that changes host behavior.
failure.check: Review discovery scope, server identity, tool permissions, and output handling.
failure.fix: Limit exposed tools and validate returned data before use.

experiment.change: Change the server deployment or tool allowlist for a representative client.
experiment.observe: Observe discovery, authentication, call reliability, and output safety.
experiment.limit: The right hosting choice depends on the tool’s runtime and operational needs.

masteryQuestion: What does MCP standardize, and what remains the host’s responsibility?
masteryAnswer: It standardizes interaction patterns. The host still owns tool selection, identity, authorization, validation, and safe output handling.

title: Deployment by workload
principle: Deployment choice must match traffic, control, and performance needs.
mechanism: Compare on-demand invocation, provisioned throughput, and hosted endpoints against usage pattern, latency, model control, and operations.Include cold starts and peak periods in the workload profile.

decision.when: Use this skill when moving an FM capability into a production application.
decision.choice: Select a deployment option using measured workload requirements.
decision.reason: The option should handle expected demand without unnecessary operations or cost.
decision.reject: Reject choosing solely from a prototype’s low-volume behavior.

workedTrace: An application has variable user demand.
The team measures request pattern and latency requirements.
It selects an invocation or endpoint approach suited to the workload.
Monitoring verifies behavior under representative traffic.

failure.symptom: A deployment works in a demo but throttles or costs too much under actual traffic.
failure.check: Compare real request profile, capacity, quotas, and endpoint configuration.
failure.fix: Tune deployment capacity or choose a better-fitting option.

experiment.change: Change deployment mode while holding request and workload profile constant.
experiment.observe: Observe latency, availability, scaling behavior, and cost signals.
experiment.limit: Service options and limits can vary by model and Region.

masteryQuestion: What workload evidence should guide deployment selection?
masteryAnswer: Traffic shape, latency needs, capacity behavior, model control, and operating constraints.

title: LLM deployment constraints
principle: LLM serving has resource behavior tied to model loading, memory, accelerator use, and token processing.
mechanism: Plan artifact loading, memory capacity, concurrency, request length, and generation limits for the chosen serving pattern.

decision.when: Use this skill when hosting or configuring large models on managed compute.
decision.choice: Profile the model and workload under expected input and output shapes.
decision.reason: Token work and model size affect resource use differently from many conventional services.
decision.reject: Reject scaling plans based only on request count.

workedTrace: A hosted model receives long prompts and generates responses.
The runtime loads model weights and allocates device memory.
Concurrency and token lengths raise active resource demand.
The endpoint queues or fails when capacity is inadequate.

failure.symptom: Endpoint capacity appears sufficient by request rate but fails on large contexts.
failure.check: Measure token lengths, memory pressure, loading time, and accelerator utilization.
failure.fix: Adjust model placement, capacity, or request limits using profile evidence.

experiment.change: Change the maximum input or output token budget in a test workload.
experiment.observe: Observe memory use, throughput, latency, and quality effects.
experiment.limit: Reducing token limits can harm task completeness.

masteryQuestion: Why is request count alone a weak capacity measure for LLM serving?
masteryAnswer: Requests can differ in token length and generation work, which changes resource demand.

title: Deployment optimization
principle: Deployment optimization balances quality, latency, cost, and resource use.
mechanism: Use smaller task-fit models, model cascades, caching, or API routes where evaluation supports the change.

decision.when: Use this skill when a valid system needs lower cost or faster response.
decision.choice: Optimize the bottleneck or call type shown by measurement.
decision.reason: Targeted routing can reserve stronger models for requests that need them.
decision.reject: Reject reducing model quality globally without measuring task impact.

workedTrace: A simple request reaches a high-capability model.
A classifier or lightweight route identifies a routine task.
Routine work uses a smaller adequate model while complex cases escalate.
Evaluation checks quality across both routes.

failure.symptom: The cascade sends difficult questions to the weak model or adds more calls than it saves.
failure.check: Inspect route decisions, escalation, per-class quality, and total calls.
failure.fix: Revise routing criteria or remove the cascade if gains do not hold.

experiment.change: Change the cascade threshold or task routing rule in a test set.
experiment.observe: Observe task quality, calls per request, latency, and cost.
experiment.limit: A cascade adds routing errors and needs coverage for misclassified tasks.

masteryQuestion: When is a model cascade useful?
masteryAnswer: When a measured workload has simpler requests that a smaller model handles adequately and complex cases can escalate safely.

title: Enterprise connectivity
principle: Enterprise connectivity links FM services with existing data, identity, and business systems.
mechanism: Use APIs, events, or synchronization to connect systems while preserving ownership, permissions, and failure recovery.

decision.when: Use this skill when AI features need legacy records or enterprise workflows.
decision.choice: Use a loose integration boundary with explicit contracts and change handling.
decision.reason: It limits coupling and provides a controlled path for data exchange.
decision.reject: Reject direct database access that bypasses the system’s data rules.

workedTrace: A legacy system owns a service record.
An integration API retrieves permitted fields for a caller.
The AI workflow uses those fields to form a response.
A trace links the answer to the source record and integration result.

failure.symptom: The application receives stale or overbroad enterprise data.
failure.check: Check source ownership, API scope, synchronization age, and access controls.
failure.fix: Narrow the integration and define update and failure behavior.

experiment.change: Change the data integration from a broad export to a scoped API request.
experiment.observe: Observe field minimization, freshness, and failure isolation.
experiment.limit: Enterprise interfaces can impose latency and availability dependencies.

masteryQuestion: What should an AI integration preserve when connecting to a legacy system?
masteryAnswer: Data ownership, access rules, field scope, update behavior, and a recoverable error contract.

title: Application integration
principle: GenAI integration adds model capability to an existing application through stable service boundaries.
mechanism: Use APIs, webhooks, events, or microservices to invoke model workflows without coupling user interfaces to provider details.

decision.when: Use this skill when adding GenAI behavior to an existing product or process.
decision.choice: Expose an application-level API with validation and consistent response states.
decision.reason: A stable boundary lets the application control identity, errors, and version changes.
decision.reject: Reject placing model credentials or provider logic in a client interface.

workedTrace: A user submits a request through an existing application.
The backend validates the caller and invokes a GenAI service.
The service returns a result or controlled error.
The application presents output and records a trace identifier.

failure.symptom: The UI hangs on a model timeout or exposes provider credentials.
failure.check: Inspect client-server boundaries, auth, timeouts, and error mapping.
failure.fix: Keep credentials server-side and implement explicit timeout behavior.

experiment.change: Change the integration from direct client invocation to a backend API.
experiment.observe: Observe credential exposure, error handling, and application compatibility.
experiment.limit: An API gateway or Lambda integration does not automatically solve application semantics.

masteryQuestion: Where should model credentials and provider-specific logic reside?
masteryAnswer: In a controlled backend integration, not in an exposed client application.

title: Secure access framework
principle: Secure access controls which identities can invoke models and reach supporting data or tools.
mechanism: Use federation, roles, resource policies, and least privilege. Enforce user-level data access within retrieval and application logic.

decision.when: Use this skill when enterprise identities cross application and model service boundaries.
decision.choice: Map authenticated enterprise identity to scoped AWS and application permissions.
decision.reason: Separate roles and permissions limit impact if a component is misused.
decision.reject: Reject a shared powerful role for all users and actions.

workedTrace: An employee authenticates through enterprise federation.
The application maps identity to an approved role and data scope.
The request invokes only allowed models and retrieval filters.
Audit records capture the action and principal.

failure.symptom: A user can invoke a model or retrieve records outside their role.
failure.check: Trace identity claims, role policy, resource policy, and query filters.
failure.fix: Remove broad permissions and bind data filters to trusted identity.

experiment.change: Change a shared role into task-specific least-privilege roles.
experiment.observe: Observe denied unauthorized actions and preserved allowed tasks.
experiment.limit: IAM service permissions alone do not enforce every document-level rule.

masteryQuestion: How should an enterprise identity affect a RAG request?
masteryAnswer: It should determine allowed service actions and trusted record filters before content reaches the model.

title: Cross-environment compliance
principle: Cross-environment design connects cloud, on-premises, and edge systems while respecting data boundaries.
mechanism: Map where data is stored, processed, routed, and logged. Use suitable private connectivity or edge placement for the stated requirement.

decision.when: Use this skill when jurisdiction, latency, or local data handling constrains FM access.
decision.choice: Keep sensitive data within the allowed boundary and move only approved content.
decision.reason: Data location and path determine whether the design meets compliance needs.
decision.reject: Reject assuming network connectivity alone satisfies jurisdictional policy.

workedTrace: A source record must remain in an approved environment.
A local component extracts only allowed fields.
A secure route sends approved content to an available inference service.
Logs and outputs follow the same location and retention rules.

failure.symptom: Data or logs cross a boundary that policy prohibits.
failure.check: Trace all data paths, regions, endpoints, and logging destinations.
failure.fix: Remove or relocate the violating path and verify each destination.

experiment.change: Change the inference path to process sensitive content at an approved location.
experiment.observe: Observe data movement, latency, and retained copies.
experiment.limit: Compliance requirements depend on the organization’s rules and applicable service availability.

masteryQuestion: What must be mapped in a cross-environment AI design?
masteryAnswer: Data location, processing, network path, logs, outputs, identity, and retention.

title: GenAI CI/CD and gateway
principle: Enterprise gateways control model access, while CI/CD controls how changes reach those gateways and applications.
mechanism: Version prompts and routes, scan code and infrastructure, run evaluations, apply policy checks, and retain rollback state.

decision.when: Use this skill when many teams consume FM services under shared security and compliance rules.
decision.choice: Combine a centralized consumption boundary with repeatable release gates.
decision.reason: It provides common controls and makes changes traceable.
decision.reject: Reject a gateway without governance or a pipeline without behavior checks.

workedTrace: A team proposes a prompt and route change.
CI validates configuration, security, and evaluation evidence.
An approved release updates the gateway policy or application.
Monitoring detects regression and rollback restores the prior version.

failure.symptom: An untested prompt or route reaches production through a configuration edit.
failure.check: Inspect release records, approval gates, version links, and gateway logs.
failure.fix: Gate promotion on matching evidence and restrict policy change rights.

experiment.change: Change the pipeline to require evaluation for each route or prompt version.
experiment.observe: Observe blocked unapproved changes and traceable approved deployment.
experiment.limit: Automated checks cover defined cases, not all possible model behavior.

masteryQuestion: What should CI/CD validate for a GenAI gateway change?
masteryAnswer: It should validate security, policy, request contracts, relevant evaluations, approval, and rollback readiness.

title: Flexible API interaction
principle: API integration must support synchronous and asynchronous work with validated request contracts.
mechanism: Use SDK or service APIs for direct calls, queues for deferred work, and gateways for custom validation and client contracts.

decision.when: Use this skill when different workloads need different request timing or compute environments.
decision.choice: Choose synchronous calls for immediate results and asynchronous patterns for longer tasks.
decision.reason: The interaction pattern should match user wait tolerance and task duration.
decision.reject: Reject forcing all tasks through a blocking request.

workedTrace: A client submits a task that can finish quickly.
The backend validates and invokes the model synchronously.
A longer task instead enters a queue with a tracking identifier.
The client receives the result or task status through its contract.

failure.symptom: Long-running requests time out or asynchronous work loses its correlation.
failure.check: Check duration, queue state, request IDs, and result delivery.
failure.fix: Select the correct interaction pattern and persist task status.

experiment.change: Change a long task from synchronous invocation to queue-backed processing.
experiment.observe: Observe timeout rate, completion delivery, and trace continuity.
experiment.limit: Asynchronous processing adds status, retry, and duplicate handling needs.

masteryQuestion: When should an API use asynchronous processing?
masteryAnswer: When task duration or workload behavior does not fit a reliable user-facing synchronous response.

title: Real-time streaming
principle: Streaming delivers response pieces before the full model response completes.
mechanism: Connect the model stream to server-sent events or WebSockets and handle partial, final, and error states.

decision.when: Use this skill when early visible output improves an interactive experience.
decision.choice: Stream content through a backend that can preserve authorization and completion state.
decision.reason: The user can see progress without waiting for the entire response.
decision.reject: Reject treating the first token as a completed answer.

workedTrace: The application opens an authorized streaming request.
The model emits content events over time.
The backend forwards events and tracks completion.
The UI marks the response final only after the terminal event.

failure.symptom: The UI displays partial text as final or fails to handle a midstream error.
failure.check: Inspect event order, terminal state, client disconnect, and error path.
failure.fix: Represent partial and complete states separately and show recovery behavior.

experiment.change: Change the transport from buffered response to event streaming.
experiment.observe: Observe time to first content, total completion, and disconnect handling.
experiment.limit: Streaming does not guarantee lower total latency or support for every route.

masteryQuestion: What state must a client track during a streamed response?
masteryAnswer: It must distinguish open, partial, complete, and failed states.

title: Resilient API operation
principle: Reliable API operation combines error classification, bounded recovery, and observability.
mechanism: Use SDK retry behavior for transient conditions, rate limits, timeouts, and traces across service boundaries.

decision.when: Use this skill when model calls must recover predictably from service variation.
decision.choice: Apply error-specific retry and rate controls with request tracing.
decision.reason: This avoids repeating permanent failures and reveals dependency behavior.
decision.reject: Reject retrying every error or hiding final failures from the caller.

workedTrace: A request receives a throttling response.
The SDK applies bounded backoff and records another attempt.
The service accepts a later attempt or returns a final error.
Tracing shows attempt count and final outcome.

failure.symptom: Retries increase load or a permanent error repeats.
failure.check: Inspect error class, retry policy, rate limits, and trace spans.
failure.fix: Restrict retries to transient errors and return a clear failure state.

experiment.change: Change the retry policy to exclude validation and access errors.
experiment.observe: Observe attempts, success rate, latency, and load during test faults.
experiment.limit: A timeout can leave operation status unknown, especially for side effects.

masteryQuestion: Which errors should not receive automatic retries?
masteryAnswer: Validation and access errors need correction. Retrying them cannot fix the underlying request or permission.

title: Intelligent model routing
principle: Model routing selects a route based on configuration, request features, or measured conditions.
mechanism: Keep route policy explicit, validate supported models, and preserve compatible response behavior.Log route reasons so operators can review unexpected selections.

decision.when: Use this skill when tasks vary in complexity, modality, cost, or availability.
decision.choice: Route by a known task class or rule, then evaluate each path.
decision.reason: A decision rule is inspectable and can reserve specialized models for suitable work.
decision.reject: Reject hidden routing that cannot be explained or tested.

workedTrace: A request arrives with task type and modality.
A routing rule checks allowed routes and current policy.
The selected model receives a compatible request.
The result and chosen route are recorded for evaluation.

failure.symptom: Requests route to an unsupported model or a low-capability route.
failure.check: Inspect classification, policy, model access, and per-route outcomes.
failure.fix: Add route validation and fallback behavior with explicit limits.

experiment.change: Change the routing rule for one task category.
experiment.observe: Observe route selection accuracy, task quality, and latency.
experiment.limit: Dynamic routing can introduce classification errors and needs fallback tests.

masteryQuestion: What makes an intelligent route safe to operate?
masteryAnswer: Explicit policy, validated routes, traceability, per-route evaluation, and a tested fallback.

title: FM API interface design
principle: A GenAI API must manage variable output, token limits, and failure states.
mechanism: Define request validation, context and output budgets, timeout behavior, retries, and response status. Support streaming when needed.

decision.when: Use this skill when building application-facing interfaces for model workloads.
decision.choice: Expose application-level operations with clear limits and errors.
decision.reason: Clients need stable behavior despite variable model response time and length.
decision.reject: Reject returning raw provider responses without a defined client contract.

workedTrace: A client submits a question and allowed context.
The API validates input and applies token budgets.
The service invokes inference with bounded recovery.
The response returns content, completion state, and trace reference.

failure.symptom: Oversized input, timeout, or partial output breaks client behavior.
failure.check: Check validation, budget calculation, terminal state, and error mapping.
failure.fix: Enforce limits before inference and return explicit partial or failed status.

experiment.change: Change the request token budget or timeout policy in a test environment.
experiment.observe: Observe rejection behavior, latency, and response completeness.
experiment.limit: Budgets and limits must reflect model support and task needs.

masteryQuestion: What should a custom FM API expose beyond answer text?
masteryAnswer: It should define request limits, completion or failure state, and useful trace information.

title: Accessible AI interfaces
principle: Accessible interfaces lower integration effort through clear contracts and usable workflow components.
mechanism: Use declarative UI, API specifications, or workflow builders while retaining backend authorization and validation.

decision.when: Use this skill when user teams need a supported path to invoke AI capability.
decision.choice: Publish an API-first contract and accessible interface elements for the intended users.
decision.reason: A stable interface supports adoption without exposing service internals.
decision.reject: Reject a no-code surface that bypasses policy or hides error states.

workedTrace: A product team publishes an OpenAPI contract for an AI operation.
A UI invokes the contract through an authenticated backend.
The backend validates input and returns explicit states.
Users can understand success, uncertainty, or required correction.

failure.symptom: Users cannot tell whether output is incomplete, invalid, or awaiting review.
failure.check: Test interface states, accessibility needs, auth flow, and API errors.
failure.fix: Add clear status and validation behavior at the user boundary.

experiment.change: Change the interface to show a distinct review or incomplete state.
experiment.observe: Observe task completion and user correction behavior.
experiment.limit: A friendly interface cannot make unsafe backend behavior safe.

masteryQuestion: What makes an AI interface accessible and safe to integrate?
masteryAnswer: A clear contract, usable interaction, explicit status, and backend-enforced controls.

title: Business system enhancement
principle: Business enhancements place model capability inside an existing process with source and action controls.
mechanism: Use orchestration, webhooks, or data automation to process business records and route results to existing systems.Keep the original record available for audit and correction.

decision.when: Use this skill when GenAI should improve a CRM, document workflow, or operations task.
decision.choice: Start with a bounded workflow step and preserve the system of record.
